books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text:
Thomas Jefferson, retired at Monticello, wrote to Congressman John Holmes about the Missouri question on April 22, 1820:

“but this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror. I considered it at once as the knell of the Union. it is hushed indeed for the moment. but this is a reprieve only, not a final sentence. a geographical line, coinciding with a marked principle, moral and political, once conceived and held up to the angry passions of men, will never be obliterated; and every new irritation will mark it deeper and deeper.”
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820; text verified against Founders Online and the Library of Congress. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Jefferson to John Holmes, April 22, 1820 (public domain, verified against Founders Online)
stem: A historian using this letter as evidence about the Missouri crisis should keep in mind that

options.text: Jefferson wrote the letter to persuade Congress to pass the Compromise in March 1820
options.misconception: The letter is private, to one congressman, written after the Compromise passed in March 1820.

options.text: the letter proves most Americans shared Jefferson’s fear
options.misconception: One man’s private fear proves one man’s fear; it cannot stand in for most Americans.

options.text: Jefferson’s words show the Compromise was unpopular in the South
options.misconception: The letter shows Jefferson’s fear of division, not Southern opinion about the Compromise.

options.text: Jefferson wrote privately as a retired president, so the letter shows personal fear

rationales.A: The Compromise passed in March 1820, and this private letter to Holmes is dated April 22. A letter written after a vote cannot persuade Congress to take it.
rationales.B: Jefferson speaks for himself here, a retired president writing privately. One letter never proves what most Americans thought.
rationales.C: Jefferson worries the line will divide the country, but he says nothing about how Southerners judged the Compromise. Do not read their opinion into his fear.
rationales.D: Jefferson writes as a private citizen at Monticello, not as a president or a congressman. That makes the letter strong evidence of his own alarm and weak evidence of official policy.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who is writing and to whom. A retired president, writing privately to one congressman.
2. Ask when. April 22, 1820, after the Compromise passed, so it cannot be lobbying for the vote.
3. Ask what the letter can show. A private letter shows what its writer felt and feared.
4. Ask what it cannot show. It cannot show official policy, Southern opinion, or what most Americans thought.
Background: Jefferson had left the presidency in 1809 and lived at Monticello; Holmes was a Massachusetts congressman who had voted against restricting slavery in Missouri.
Remember: a source’s author, audience, and date set what it can and cannot prove.
